Can wearable signals flag nurse stress? Findings from the Nurse Stress Dataset

Data Analyst (R) technical assessment

Summary

Wrist-worn Empatica E4 data from 15 hospital nurses (609 session files, about 1,250 hours) were matched to the stress level each nurse reported for specific work periods. After allowing for which nurse was recording, average skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature and movement did not reliably separate high-stress from lower-stress periods. Differences between nurses mattered more than differences in the signals. A wrist band alone is therefore a weak stress marker; personalised baselines are worth testing.

Data and methods

Signals and units.

Name Full name Unit Native rate
EDA Electrodermal activity (skin conductance) microsiemens (uS) 4 Hz
HR Heart rate beats per minute (bpm) 1 Hz
TEMP Skin temperature degrees Celsius 4 Hz
ACC (acc_mag) Accelerometer movement magnitude g (converted from raw counts) 32 Hz
Stress level Stress level reported by the nurse 0, 1, 2 one value per survey window

Blood volume pulse (BVP), inter-beat interval (IBI) and button tags were not used. The participant called “E4” is a nurse ID and not the wristband.

File structure. Each nurse has a folder of session zips. Each zip holds EDA, HR, TEMP and ACC CSVs where line 1 is the Unix start time, line 2 the sample rate and the rest the data. SurveyResults.xlsx has one row per reported period: nurse ID, start and end time, date and a stress level (0, 1 or 2).

Merging. Every signal was averaged to 1 Hz (whole-second means) and outer-merged on the Unix second; the HR file starts 10 s later than the others. Each sensor second inherited the stress level of the survey window containing it (nurse ID plus start and end time, inclusive). Survey times are local hospital time, converted from America/Chicago to UTC after testing hourly offsets per nurse (see Appendix A9).

Derived features. HR_sd60 (heart rate fluctuation: standard deviation over 60 s, a short-term proxy and not clinical heart rate variability), EDA_phasic (EDA minus its trailing 30 s mean, a fast-arousal proxy), EDA_slope (EDA change per second over 10 s), 60 s rolling means of heart rate and movement, and a local time-of-day segment (Morning 06-12, Afternoon 12-18, Evening/Night otherwise). Rolling windows are computed within each session so they never span recording breaks.

Data Quality Considerations

Issue Why it matters How it was handled
Misaligned clocks Survey times are local and sensor times are UTC; unmatched labels would hide any real signal. Timezone-aware conversion chosen by testing offsets per nurse; labelled data rose from 2% to 7.9% of seconds, and the best offset is now 0 h for all 15 nurses.
Different sampling rates / offset start Signals cannot be compared second by second without a common time base. All signals averaged to 1 Hz and merged on the Unix second.
Implausible values Off-wrist or poor-contact readings look like extreme physiology. Set to NA: HR outside 30-220 bpm (none found), skin temperature outside 25-42 C (22,202 s, all below 25 C), EDA outside 0.01-60 uS (128,973 s, 2.9%, all below 0.01 uS). The upper limits never triggered.
Duplicate sensor records Overlapping sessions repeat seconds and overweight them. 1,501 duplicate nurse-seconds removed; none remain.
Missing values Gaps could bias rolling features. Under 0.15% missing per signal; gaps of 5 s or less forward-filled, longer left as NA.
Irregular sampling Gaps break rolling windows. No gaps over 5 s within any session. All 609 session files loaded.
Scaling Raw accelerometer counts are not interpretable. Raw counts divided by 64 to give g; median 1.004 g at rest.
Surveys without sensor data A stress level with no sensor data cannot be analysed. 28 of 242 distinct windows have no sensor data. They cluster by date (for example nurse 15 on 17 July 2020), which points to missing recordings and not clock error. Excluded from modelling.
Duplicate survey rows Two rows for one window could double-count it or contradict each other. 3 exact duplicates (7A rows 39 and 52; F5 rows 167 and 169; F5 rows 170 and 171). The higher row number is kept; no label lost or contradicted. Two partial overlaps (6B, E4) carry the same level in both rows.
Surveys with no stress level These rows cannot define the outcome. 113 of 358 survey rows hold ‘na’ in the stress-level column and were dropped; the cause is not stated in the data.
Sparse labels Only a small share of recorded time has a stress label. 7.9% of seconds labelled (3.7% to 21.4% per nurse). Modelling uses labelled windows only.

Survey accounting. 358 rows in the sheet; 113 without a stress level leaves 245 numeric rows; removing 3 duplicates leaves 242 distinct windows; 28 have no sensor data, leaving the 214 windows that were modelled.

Correlation heatmap

Spearman correlation on 1-minute epochs, with pairwise deletion of missing values. Spearman was chosen because EDA and movement are skewed with outliers and relationships need only be monotonic. The stress row uses labelled epochs only. Every epoch counts equally here, so long survey windows weigh more than short ones; the model below weights each window once, so the two are not directly comparable.

Spearman correlation of signals, derived features and reported stress.

  • Skin temperature and EDA move together (rho 0.47), mostly reflecting wear and warmth.
  • EDA_phasic and EDA_slope are almost the same measure (rho 0.91), so only EDA_phasic entered the model.
  • Every correlation with reported stress is weak (|rho| of 0.13 or less; skin temperature highest).

Statistical analysis

Hypothesis. H0: mean physiology during a survey window is unrelated to the window being rated high stress (level 2), after accounting for nurse. H1: higher arousal markers raise the odds of a high-stress window. Tests are two-sided at the 0.05 level.

Method. Mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept per nurse, one row per survey window (214 windows with at least 3 one-minute epochs; 161 high stress, 53 not), predictors scaled to 1 SD. Windows last 3 to 324 minutes (median 16) and each counts once. The label is constant within a window, so the window, not the minute, is the unit of analysis. A first model on minute-level rows with a nested window effect was rejected because the random effect absorbed the outcome (ICC 1.0).

Assumption checks. Variance inflation at most 1.45 (below 5: no collinearity concern); the model converged with no singular fit; binned residuals 80% inside bounds (95% preferred), so calibration is imperfect.

Measure Odds ratio per 1 SD 95% CI low 95% CI high p
Skin conductance (EDA) 1.36 0.89 2.06 0.15
Heart rate 0.78 0.52 1.18 0.24
Skin temperature 1.08 0.69 1.70 0.73
Movement 0.82 0.56 1.22 0.33
EDA short-term change 0.88 0.55 1.42 0.60
Heart rate fluctuation (1-min SD) 1.04 0.70 1.56 0.83

Odds ratios per 1 SD; 1 means no effect.

Plain-language reading. No signal was statistically significant and every interval includes 1. Skin conductance came closest (odds 1.36 per SD, 95% CI 0.89 to 2.06). Physiology explains about 5% of the variation in whether a window was high stress (marginal R2 0.046); adding nurse identity brings it to 21% (conditional R2 0.211, ICC 0.17).

Insights

  1. Wrist signals alone are weak stress markers. Correlations with reported stress are at most 0.13, and the window-level model is null.
  2. Who the nurse is matters more than the physiology. About 17% of the variation in high versus lower stress windows sits between nurses, versus about 5% from the signals, which supports personalised baselines over one threshold for everyone.
  3. Reports are skewed and sparse. 73% of distinct usable surveys (177 of 242) report the top stress level and only 7.9% of recorded time is labelled, which limits contrast for any model.

Limitations and next steps

Only 214 labelled windows (53 not high stress) for six predictors, about 8.8 events per predictor; a single report per period; a dichotomised outcome (cutoff at level 2, level 1 sensitivity not yet run); window averages lose within-window dynamics and long windows (up to 324 minutes) count once like short ones; Cook’s distance flagged 13 windows but is unreliable for mixed logistic models; associations only. Most cutoffs below were not varied to test sensitivity, and the upper limits on temperature and EDA never triggered. Next: nurse-specific baselines, the survey’s stressor categories (for example patient crisis or workload), and validation on new nurses.

Appendix A: Assumptions

ID Stage Assumption Justification Risk
A1 Loading One zip is one recording session; nurse ID is the filename prefix before ’_’. Folder and file names match survey IDs; all 15 IDs matched. Low.
A2 Loading Each CSV: line 1 Unix start (UTC seconds), line 2 sample rate (Hz), then data; sample i is timed start + (i-1)/rate. Matches the file contents inspected and the Dryad description. Time shift if the device clock drifted.
A3 Loading Each signal reduced to 1 Hz by the mean of all samples in each whole second. HR is 1 Hz, so 1 Hz is the common resolution without inventing HR data. Loses within-second detail.
A4 Loading Outer merge on the Unix second; HR starts 10 s after the other files, giving NA at session starts. Visible in the file headers. Slightly more missing HR (0.14%).
A5 Loading Movement = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2) / 64, in g; raw accelerometer values taken to be 1/64 g counts. Checked empirically: median 1.004 g at rest (range 0.39 to 2.87 g). Wrong scale changes units, not correlations or odds ratios per SD.
A6 Loading Duplicate (nurse, second) rows from overlapping sessions dropped, first kept (4,506,559 to 4,505,058 rows). A second can have one reading only. Duplicates may differ slightly.
A7 Loading Unreadable zips are skipped with a console message and do not stop the run. Stops one bad file halting the run; all 609 zips loaded. None in practice (609 of 609 loaded).
A8 Survey Only the first Excel sheet read (358 rows; the workbook has a single sheet); rows whose stress level is not numeric dropped (358 to 245). The only sheet covers all 15 IDs; the 113 dropped rows hold the text ‘na’. Cause of the 113 missing levels unknown; nothing assumed about them.
A9 Survey Survey times are local hospital time (America/Chicago, daylight-saving aware) and converted to UTC; sensors are UTC. First test, treating survey times as UTC: UTC-5 best for most nurses (summer), UTC-6 for 7E, 83, BG (after 1 Nov). After conversion, offset 0 is best for all 15 nurses (217 surveys overlap sensor data at 0 h versus 163 at +1 h); EG ties across -2 to 0 h on 4 surveys and offset 0 has the most rows. Hourly test only; sub-hour drift untested.
A10 Survey Excel dummy date 1899-12-31 ignored (clock time only); a window ending before it starts crosses midnight. Visible in the file structure. Wrong date if typed incorrectly.
A11 Labelling Every sensor second inside a survey window (inclusive) inherits its stress level; on overlap the higher row number in the sheet overwrites (not the later in time). A survey describes its whole window. Label may hold for only part of the window. Five overlaps (about 3,300 s, under 1% of labelled time) all carry the same level in both rows.
A12 Outcome Stress levels 0, 1, 2 are increasing intensity; ‘high stress’ = 2, ‘not high’ = 0 or 1. Coding is inferred. Of 242 distinct numeric rows: 177 level 2, 19 level 1, 46 level 0; level 1 too small to stand alone. Different coding would blur the outcome; level 1 sensitivity not run.
A13 Quality Implausible readings set to NA, not deleted, to preserve timing. Keeps rolling windows aligned. Over-strict limits drop real data.
A14 Features Gaps of 5 s or less forward-filled within a session; longer gaps left as NA. Short dropouts unlikely to change physiology; no gaps over 5 s exist. Minimal.
A15 Features Rolling windows are trailing and computed within a session. Windows must not span recording breaks. First 59 s of a session have no 60 s feature.
A16 Features EDA_phasic is a simple proxy (EDA minus trailing 30 s mean), not a formal tonic/phasic decomposition; HR_sd60 uses the population formula. Fast, transparent, reproducible. Cruder than model-based decomposition.
A17 Features day_part uses local Chicago hour from the first second of an epoch; computed but not used in the model. Standard shift-like segments. None for conclusions.
A18 Epochs A 1-minute epoch is the mean per floor(second/60) per session; its label is the first non-missing label in that minute. Reduces autocorrelation and data size. An epoch can straddle a window edge.
A19 Modelling Unit of analysis is the survey window (epochs averaged per nurse and survey); at least 3 one-minute epochs (counted whether or not every signal is present); windows with a missing predictor mean dropped. The label is constant within a window, so minutes are not independent. None in practice: all 214 windows have 3 or more epochs (median 16, maximum 324), so the rule removed nothing.
A20 Modelling Predictors z-scored across the 214 windows (odds ratios per 1 SD); random nurse intercept assumed normal. Common scale; repeated windows per nurse. Between-nurse and within-nurse changes not separated (no within-nurse centring).
A21 Modelling EDA_slope excluded from the model; EDA_phasic kept. Spearman rho 0.91 between them. None for conclusions.

Appendix B: Cutoffs and parameters

Parameter Value Basis
Heart rate plausible range 30 to 220 bpm Physiological limits; no values fell outside.
Skin temperature plausible range 25 to 42 degrees C Below 25 suggests off-wrist; 22,202 s removed, all below 25; none above 42.
EDA plausible range 0.01 to 60 uS Below 0.01 is consistent with no skin contact (not tested); 128,973 s (2.9%) removed, all below 0.01; none above 60 or 100 uS, so the upper limit never triggered.
Gap flagged as irregular more than 5 s None found within sessions.
Forward-fill limit 5 s See A14.
Rolling windows HR mean 60 s, HR SD 60 s, EDA mean 30 s, movement 60 s See A15.
EDA slope lag 10 s Short-term change.
Epoch length 60 s See A18.
Daily segments (local time) 06-12, 12-18, otherwise Evening/Night See A17.
Survey clock America/Chicago to UTC See A9.
Outcome cutoff (STRESS_CUT) 2 See A12.
Minimum epochs per window (MIN_EPOCHS) 3 See A19.
Correlation method Spearman, pairwise deletion Skewed signals; monotonic relationships.
Significance level 0.05, two-sided Wald z; no correction for six tests Standard default; exploratory.
Confidence intervals 95%, Wald broom.mixed default.
Optimiser bobyqa, Laplace approximation Stable convergence.
Collinearity check VIF below 5 acceptable (maximum 1.45) performance package default.
Residual check about 95% of binned residuals inside bounds desired (observed 80%) performance package default.
Outlier check Cook’s distance 0.9 performance default; unreliable for mixed logistic models.

Appendix C: Reconciliation and open items

Resolved by re-running every script from scratch (all outputs reproduced exactly).

  1. All 609 session zips loaded; no session skipped.
  2. The survey workbook has one sheet; the 113 dropped rows contain ‘na’ as the stress level.
  3. The 31 surveys without labelled seconds are 28 with no sensor data plus 3 duplicate rows overwritten in overlaps.
  4. The clock offset is 0 h for all 15 nurses.
  5. The temperature and EDA upper limits never triggered; all removals were low readings.
  6. The 3-epoch rule removed no windows.

Still open.

  1. The stress-level coding (A12) is inferred, and the cause of the 113 ‘na’ rows is not stated in the data.
  2. Level 1 sensitivity (cutoff at level 1) has not been run.
  3. Whether the 28 missing recordings are device failures or upload gaps cannot be determined from the files.
